intro.html: Clubs, schools, towns and kingdoms all need ways to make rules and to unmake them. This topic’s words describe each step: a rule is enacted or decreed, written as a statute, approved (ratified) or blocked (vetoed), and later perhaps repealed, rescinded, abolished or nullified. These words appear constantly in history passages.

Making rules: enact (make into law), statute (a written law), mandate (an official order; also, authority from voters), decree (a ruler’s order), ratify (formally approve). Blocking and unmaking: veto (a power to reject), abolish (end completely), repeal (cancel a law), rescind (take back an order or offer), nullify (make void).

words.ex: The town council {enacted} a rule requiring dogs to be leashed in the park.
words.ctx: After years of debate, the state finally {enacted} the safety law, and by the next spring every new school bus had seat belts.
words.etym: From en (into) + act, a law passed by a lawmaking body: to put into an act.
words.note: Enact can also mean to act out: “The class enacted the signing of the treaty.”

mn.cue: EN-ACT: turn a plan INTO an ACT (a law)
mn.text: The town council votes yes, and the mayor signs the new leash rule with a flourish: now it is an official act. To make a plan into law is to {enact} it.

scene.alt: A woman signs a new leash law into effect while a boy and his dog look on.

words.ex: A {statute} passed by the state lawmakers last spring bans fireworks after ten o’clock at night.
words.ctx: The judge explained that she could not simply follow her own sense of fairness; she had to apply the {statute} exactly as the lawmakers had written it.
words.etym: From Latin statutum, “something set up,” from statuere, “to set up, to decide.”
words.note: A statute (a law) is not a statue (a sculpture) or stature (height, or standing).

mn.text: In front of the courthouse, a stone statue holds up a scroll: the town’s first written law. The statue is art; the scroll is a {statute}.

scene.alt: A woman points to a stone statue holding a scroll; the statue is labeled statue and the scroll statute.

words.def: an official order; also, authority given by voters
words.ex: The school board issued a {mandate}: every student must wear a helmet on the bike path.
words.ctx: Having won the election with eighty percent of the vote, the new mayor believed she had a clear {mandate} to rebuild the old park.
words.etym: From Latin mandatum, “something ordered,” from mandare, “to order, to entrust.”

mn.text: The principal posts the new command by the bike path: “Helmets required.” An official order like that is a {mandate}.

scene.alt: A principal points to a helmets-required sign as a boy with a helmet stands by his bike.

words.def: an official order from a ruler or authority
words.ex: By royal {decree}, the last Friday in June became a holiday.
words.ctx: The king’s {decree} was read aloud in every village square: from that day on, no one could cut wood in the royal forest without permission.
words.etym: From Latin decretum, “something decided,” from decernere, “to decide”: de (from) + cernere (to sift, to decide).

mn.cue: de-CREE: the king DECIDES, all AGREE
mn.text: The king raises his scepter: “From now on, every Friday is ice-cream day!” The king decides, and everyone must agree. A ruler’s official order is a {decree}.

scene.alt: A king raises his scepter and declares ice-cream Fridays while children cheer.

words.def: to formally approve an agreement or plan
words.ex: The club members voted to {ratify} the new rules.
words.ctx: The treaty was signed in the spring, but it did not take effect until each nation’s lawmakers had voted to {ratify} it that winter.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin ratificare, “to confirm,” from ratus, “fixed, settled.”

mn.cue: RAT-ify: every RAT’s paw says YES
mn.text: The rats hold a meeting on their new cheese-sharing rules, and every paw goes up. When a group formally approves an agreement, they {ratify} it.

scene.alt: Three rats leap up together to approve a scroll of rules, with cheese nearby.

words.def: the power to reject a decision or law, or such a rejection
words.ex: Mom used her {veto} on our plan to adopt a goat.
words.ctx: The council voted to build the new road, but the mayor used her {veto}, and the project stopped until the council could gather enough votes to override it.

mn.text: The kids vote three to nothing to adopt a goat, but Mom holds up one hand: “I forbid it.” That single blocking vote is a {veto}.

scene.alt: Children hold up a sign asking for a goat, and their mother blocks the plan.

words.def: to end something officially, completely and for good
words.ex: The school {abolished} its old rule against wearing hats in the hallway.
words.ctx: The town {abolished} the toll on the old bridge, so drivers no longer had to stop and drop a quarter in the box every time they crossed the river.
words.etym: From French abolir, from Latin abolere, “to destroy, to do away with.”

mn.text: The town bowls over the old toll gate on the bridge: no more stopping, no more paying, gone for good. To end something completely is to {abolish} it.

scene.alt: A giant bowling ball knocks over the old toll gate by the bridge while a man cheers.

words.ex: The city {repealed} its old ban on skateboards in the park.
words.ctx: The rule against bringing snacks into the library proved so unpopular that the board {repealed} it after just one month.
words.etym: From Old French rapeler, “to call back”: re (back) + apeler (to call).

mn.cue: re-PEEL: PEEL the old rule off the wall
mn.text: A worker peels the old “NO SKATEBOARDS” sign right off the park wall, and the skaters cheer. To officially cancel a law is to {repeal} it.

scene.alt: A worker pulls down a no-skateboards sign in the park as a skater cheers.

words.def: to take back or cancel an order, offer or decision
words.ex: The coach {rescinded} the extra laps after the team apologized.
words.ctx: The company offered Jamal the job, then {rescinded} the offer a week later when it discovered it could not afford to hire anyone new.
words.etym: From Latin rescindere, “to cut off, to annul”: re (back) + scindere (to cut).

mn.cue: re-SCIND: CUT the order back off
mn.text: Ms. Ada writes HOMEWORK on the board, then the class wins the spelling bee, and she crosses it right off. To take back an order is to {rescind} it.

scene.alt: A teacher crosses out a homework assignment while her students cheer.

words.def: to make legally void; to cancel out
words.ctx: Dev scored twice, but a penalty {nullified} the second goal, and the game ended in a tie.
words.etym: From Latin nullus, “none,” + -ify: to make into nothing.

mn.cue: NULL-ify: make it NULL, worth ZERO
mn.text: Dev’s goal flies in, but the referee blows her whistle and waves it off: offside. The goal now counts for zero; she has {nullified} it.

scene.alt: A referee waves off a goal; the shocked player sees the scoreboard stay at zero.

head: step
words
rows: enact; the law is a statute
repeal (a law), rescind (an order or offer), nullify (make void), abolish (end entirely)

after.html: Three look-alikes: a statute is a law, a statue is a sculpture, and stature is height or standing. And keep the direction straight: ratify approves; repeal and rescind undo.

items.q: Which sentence uses the right word?
choices: The new statute limits parking downtown to two hours.
A bronze statute of the founder stands in the square.
She grew in statute as a leader.
items.why: A statute is a written law. A sculpture is a statue, and a person’s standing is stature.

items.q: Which word means to formally approve, not to undo?
items.why: Ratify approves an agreement. Repeal, rescind and nullify all cancel or undo.

items.q: True or false: veto comes from Latin for “I forbid.”
items.why: True. A veto is the power to block, from Latin veto, I forbid.

items.q: The college offered Ada a scholarship, then took the offer back. The college ______ the offer.
items.why: To take back an offer or order is to rescind it.
